prayer.text: Saint Rita of Cascia, pray for us.

cues.text: A Peacemaker's Daughter
Born in 1381 at Roccaporena, near Cascia in Umbria, Rita was the only child of parents renowned for reconciling local feuds.
They were nicknamed the 'Peacemakers of Jesus Christ.'
Though Rita longed from childhood to become a nun, her parents arranged her marriage at only twelve years old to a man of harsh and violent temper.
An Abusive Marriage Endured with Patience

For eighteen years Rita bore a difficult marriage marked by her husband's cruelty and infidelity, raising their two sons while quietly maintaining her own devotion and, by tradition, working to win her husband's eventual reform through patience rather than confrontation.
Her husband was ultimately murdered in a feud, a killing tied to the very kind of local vendetta her own parents had spent their lives trying to end.
A Mother's Desperate Prayer
When Rita's her two sons resolved to avenge their father's death, she pleaded with them to abandon the plan, fearing for both the lives of their intended victims and the state of her sons' own souls.

According to tradition, both young men fell seriously ill and died before they could carry out the revenge — a resolution Rita accepted as an answer, however painful, to her fervent prayers that they not become murderers themselves.
Rejected, Then Received
Widowed and childless, Rita sought to fulfill her lifelong desire for religious life at the Augustinian convent of Santa Maria Maddalena in Cascia.
But she was refused admission — by one account because the community, wary of ongoing local feuds, would not accept anyone connected to a family vendetta.
Rita is said to have first worked to reconcile her husband's family with their rivals, achieving a formal peace, before finally being accepted into the convent at around age thirty-six.
The Wound of the Thorn
As a nun, Rita became known for extraordinary austerity and deep meditation on Christ's Passion.
According to tradition, after hearing a sermon on the crown of thorns, she received a small but persistent wound on her forehead.
Said to be from one of the thorns, she bore it, painful and visible, for the last fifteen years of her life.
The Church came to see the mark as an outward sign of her intimate union with Christ's suffering.
Legacy
Rita died at Cascia in 1457 and was canonized in 1900 by Pope Leo XIII.
Devotion to her had flourished for centuries before her formal recognition, earning her in Spain the title 'La Santa de los Impossibles' — the saint of the impossible.
She remains one of the Church's most beloved patrons of difficult marriages, abuse survivors, and hopeless causes.
Her own life of sustained suffering became, in the memory of the faithful, a source of hope for the seemingly unanswerable prayer.
